#1 The page fully formal ETCS remarks that “with some slight modification, the theory Th(Topos) [essentially, the definition of a topos] may be rewritten so that it becomes an essentially algebraic theory” (and thus can be interpreted as a category with finite limits). I can see that this is true for all of the axioms of Th(Topos) listed on that page, with one exception.

I’ll paraphrase the axioms listed in the section “The theory of elementary toposes,” with the part that confuses me written in bold:

  • Definition: The arrows fff and ggg form a relation iff they have the same domain and, for all appropriately composable arrows hhh and iii, we have f∘h=f∘if \circ h = f \circ if∘h=f∘i and g∘h=g∘ig \circ h = g \circ ig∘h=g∘i only when h=ih = ih=i.
  • Axioms 1 and 2: Given an object YYY, we have an object P(Y)P(Y)P(Y) (the power object of YYY), an object E(Y)E(Y)E(Y), and arrows λ(Y):E(Y)→P(Y)\lambda(Y) : E(Y) \to P(Y)λ(Y):E(Y)→P(Y) and ρ(Y):E(Y)→Y\rho(Y) : E(Y) \to Yρ(Y):E(Y)→Y which form a relation.
  • Axiom 3: Given arrows f:X→Yf : X \to Yf:X→Y and g:X→Zg : X \to Zg:X→Z, if fff and ggg form a relation, then there is a unique arrow h:Z→P(Y)h : Z \to P(Y)h:Z→P(Y) such that ggg is the left arrow of a pullback of Z→hP(Y)←λ(Y)E(Y)Z \xrightarrow{h} P(Y) \xleftarrow{\lambda(Y)} E(Y)Zh​P(Y)λ(Y)​E(Y), with the top arrow kkk satisfying ρ(Y)∘k=f\rho(Y) \circ k = fρ(Y)∘k=f.

The part I don’t understand is that the premise of axiom 3 contains the predicate “fff and ggg form a relation,” which is a universal quantification. As far as I know, in an essentially algebraic theory, every axiom must be of the form “given these things, which satisfy these equations, there exist these other things, which satisfy these other equations.” There’s no mechanism that lets us put a universal quantification in the premise.

When rewriting Th(Topos) as an essentially algebraic theory, how do we get around this?
subject: The theory of a topos is an essentially algebraic theory...…

#2 (f,g) ⁣:X→Y×Z(f,g)\colon X\to Y\times Z(f,g):X→Y×Z is a relation precisely when this map is a monomorphism, and monomorphisms i ⁣:A→Bi\colon A\to Bi:A→B are characterised by a limit property: the pullback of iii along itself is the square where the other two maps are idA\mathrm{id}_AidA​.

I’m not sure I can off the top of my head go from this to answer the question completely in the spirit of talking about theories via axioms and syntax/quantifiers though. Here’s my thinking, using internal categories.

Suppose we are trying to define an internal topos EEE in a category CCC with finite limits, so we have an object E1E_1E1​ of all morphisms, and let us assume we already have established the map E1×t,E0,tE1→E1×s,E0,sE1E_1\times_{t,E_0,t}E_1 \to E_1\times_{s,E_0,s} E_1E1​×t,E0​,t​E1​→E1​×s,E0​,s​E1​ that sends a cospan x→y←zx\to y \leftarrow zx→y←z to the span x←x×yx→zx\leftarrow x\times_y x \to zx←x×y​x→z (E0E_0E0​ being the object of objects, and s,t ⁣:E1→E0s, t\colon E_1\to E_0s,t:E1​→E0​ are the source and target maps). And we also have the map E1×s,E0,sE1→E1E_1\times_{s,E_0,s} E_1 \to E_1E1​×s,E0​,s​E1​→E1​ sending the span a←b→ca\leftarrow b \to ca←b→c to b→a×cb\to a\times cb→a×c. That is, we already know EEE is an internal category with pullbacks and binary products. Then for the span given by your fff and ggg, i.e. an element of E1×s,E0,sE1E_1\times_{s,E_0,s} E_1E1​×s,E0​,s​E1​, we do

E1×s,E0,sE1→E1→ΔE1×t,E0,tE1→E1×s,E0,sE1 E_1\times_{s,E_0,s} E_1 \to E_1 \stackrel{\Delta}{\to} E_1\times_{t,E_0,t} E_1 \to E_1\times_{s,E_0,s} E_1 E1​×s,E0​,s​E1​→E1​→ΔE1​×t,E0​,t​E1​→E1​×s,E0​,s​E1​

and then we pull the map E0→E0→E1×s,E0,sE1E_0 \to E_0 \to E_1\times_{s,E_0,s} E_1E0​→E0​→E1​×s,E0​,s​E1​ (sending an object xxx to the span x←x→xx\leftarrow x \to xx←x→x of identity arrows) along this. The vertex of this pullback, E1×s,E0,sE1)×E1×s,E0,sE1E0E_1\times_{s,E_0,s} E_1)\times_{E_1\times_{s,E_0,s} E_1} E_0E1​×s,E0​,s​E1​)×E1​×s,E0​,s​E1​​E0​, is the object of jointly monic spans, that is, the object RelE\mathrm{Rel}_ERelE​ (in CCC) of “relations in EEE”.

Then Axiom 3 says there is the data of an arrow RelE→E1\mathrm{Rel}_E \to E_1RelE​→E1​ in CCC, satisfying some conditions. Note that we have a map RelE→E0\mathrm{Rel}_E\to E_0RelE​→E0​ sending (f,g) ⁣:x→y×z(f,g)\colon x\to y\times z(f,g):x→y×z to zzz. And we already posit the existence of a morphism P ⁣:E0→RelEP\colon E_0\to {\mathrm{Rel}}_EP:E0​→RelE​ that returns the universal relation on an object (so in fact it lands not just in RelE\mathrm{Rel}_ERelE​ but composes with the other projection map RelE→E0\mathrm{Rel}_E\to E_0RelE​→E0​ to give the identity (ie we have a relation out of the object we started with). I think you should be able to see your way from here to finish out the rest of the details, but I can give clarifications if the above is not clear.

#3 In general one would have to have already constructed the object CartSqE\mathrm{CartSq}_ECartSqE​ (in CCC) whose objects are cartesian squares (as a subobject of the object of commutative squares), and then the pullback map E1×t,E0,tE1→CartSqEE_1\times_{t,E_0,t} E_1 \to {\mathrm{CartSq}}_EE1​×t,E0​,t​E1​→CartSqE​ is posited, i.e. a section of the (restriction of) projection from commuting squares to cospans. One should be able to assemble this data into (or assemble it from) an internal adjunction from a suitable internal diagram category built using finite limits. Then the cospans to spans map above will be the composite E1×t,E0,tE1→CartSqE→E1×s,E0,sE1E_1\times_{t,E_0,t} E_1 \to {\mathrm{CartSq}}_E \to E_1\times_{s,E_0,s} E_1E1​×t,E0​,t​E1​→CartSqE​→E1​×s,E0​,s​E1​.

We can similarly posit the existence of a terminal object using an internal adjunction and also using data 1→E01\to E_01→E0​ with axioms. Or alternatively as a map E0→E1×t,E01E_0 \to E_1\times_{t,E_0} 1E0​→E1​×t,E0​​1, the object of arrows with codomain the terminal object, and the axiom is that should be the inverse of E1×t,E01E_1\times_{t,E_0} 1E1​×t,E0​​1.

And then from pullbacks and a terminal object all other finite limits can be built, in particular finite products.

#4

(f,g) ⁣:X→Y×Z(f,g)\colon X\to Y\times Z(f,g):X→Y×Z is a relation precisely when this map is a monomorphism, and monomorphisms i ⁣:A→Bi\colon A\to Bi:A→B are characterised by a limit property: the pullback of iii along itself is the square where the other two maps are idA\mathrm{id}_AidA​.

David, I think this completely answers my question! If I’m understanding all this correctly, we merely need to change the definition in my original post to

  • Definition: The arrows f:X→Yf : X \to Yf:X→Y and g:X→Zg : X \to Zg:X→Z form a relation iff the pullback of (f,g):X→Y×Z(f, g) : X \to Y \times Z(f,g):X→Y×Z along itself is the square where the other two maps are idX\mathrm{id}_XidX​,

and the problem goes away, since this definition is completely equational and doesn’t quantify over anything (at least not universally; existential quantification is okay here).

I feel like I should mention at this point that I’m still very much a category theory novice (I haven’t even finished Awodey’s Category Theory). None of this is totally beyond my ability to understand, but it’s all unfamiliar and there are certainly gaps in my knowledge of the fundamentals. (“Monomorphisms are characterized by a limit property” seems to be one of them!)

The remainder of your messages is on a different level from what I’ve been working at. You’re reasoning explicitly about the internal topos EEE in a category CCC; I’m attempting to reason within the internal topos while making sure that all of my reasoning can be internalized. I’m not yet fluent enough in category theory to easily be able to translate from one level to the other, so it will take me a while to understand everything you’ve written.

I’m going to take rewriting Th(Topos) as an essentially algebraic theory as a homework assignment, so to speak. I now feel like I have everything I need to attempt this, and I’m sure that everything you’ve written here will be very helpful as I’m working on it.

If I succeed, would anyone like me to write up my results as a page on nLab? It’ll be a valuable exercise for me, but I don’t know whether or not the results will be interesting to others.

Thank you for your help!

#5 Glad it helped! The reasoning I give is a different presentation of the theory, because it works in all finitely complete categories, and if you use generalised elements, you can recover the syntactic presentation.

I think that a page essentially algebraic theory of an elementary topos would not be out of place on the nLab, and can be linked from fully formal ETCS. It can include topos+NNO, of course, as a section on that page.
